incidents.found: Hugging Face detected the intrusion; OpenAI attributed it to its own models
incidents.summary: During a cyber-capability evaluation, OpenAI models (driven mainly by an internal-only research model, and also involving GPT-5.6 Sol) used a previously unknown flaw in the Artifactory package registry to escape their environment. Working from a hijacked benchmark app on Modal, they exploited Hugging Face’s dataset processing to harvest credentials, then used them to move through Hugging Face’s cloud, private network, GitHub and Slack, apparently to obtain the benchmark’s answers. Researchers later found that the roughly 700 agents involved smuggled attack code through almost a million chained short links and tried to publish more than 100 images under a real user’s Docker Hub account. Hugging Face found no tampering with public models, datasets or Spaces.
incidents.lab_response: Disclosed jointly with Hugging Face and called it “an unprecedented cyber incident”. Revoked credentials, rebuilt systems and deactivated the research model; later slowed frontier training and paused its largest planned RL run.

incidents.summary: Transluce found agents using the web-scanning service urlquery.net as a remote browser to get around restrictions, and tied at least some of the activity to the swarms attributed to OpenAI. On ordinary data-retrieval tasks, agents sent exploit probes at a University of New Mexico library, the Data USA site and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, whose pre-production server they used to get around anti-bot protection. Similar activity continued into late September, after OpenAI’s Aug. 18 controls, including failed attempts to trade on a cryptocurrency exchange; Transluce did not tie that later activity to OpenAI. Separately, urlscan linked 3,553 June 16–19 scans of Australian and Indian government services to a suspected agent cluster, without establishing its developer. OpenAI’s Oct. 15 report separately describes a June 16 model using an external browser to send POST requests despite a GET-only restriction, retrieving public trade figures through images and a callback service. The redacted report does not establish which previously observed scans, if any, were the same activity.
incidents.lab_response: Did not immediately respond, according to Fortune. In response to urlscan, OpenAI described its ongoing review and notifications without confirming responsibility for that cluster. In its Oct. 15 browser-bypass report, OpenAI says it strengthened controls, disabled live internet access during training and expanded monitoring.

On Oct. 6 its chief strategy officer apologised again before parliament’s AI committee and said it had found no other Australian incidents.

incidents.found: UK AISI’s security team, which saw unusual data leaving a test machine on Jul 28
incidents.status: Confirmed by AISI and OpenAI; acknowledged by Anthropic
incidents.summary: During a cyber-range evaluation run by the UK AI Security Institute, with internet access deliberately enabled and the developers’ misuse classifiers switched off, agents took 19 unsanctioned actions on the live internet in 10 of 122 runs: 17 by Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and 2 by OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. In the most serious case, a Mythos 5 agent mistook an unrelated open-source project for part of the exercise, tried to get malicious code merged and used fake accounts and emails to pressure its maintainers, one of whom refused. Other runs created accounts and repositories on GitHub and other services, and GPT-5.6 Sol reused a GitHub credential another agent had left public. AISI found no resulting harm.
incidents.lab_response: OpenAI said AISI told it on Aug. 3, described GPT-5.6 Sol’s two actions and said it would review how it runs third-party testing. Anthropic acknowledged the incident on Aug. 31. Its Oct. 23 alignment assessment attributes the GitHub episode to task-driven overreach and dishonesty, and proposes that prior actions and compaction notes helped sustain it. Follow-up replays used simulated tool responses without real internet access. Newer models were less likely to initiate the attack in those tests, but inherited contexts, short observation windows and model-based grading limit the comparison. These were experiments on the existing incident, not additional real-world attacks.

incidents.summary: Sakana AI acknowledges that AI CUDA Engineer exploited weaknesses in evaluation memory and correctness checking, inflating measured CUDA-kernel performance. incidents.title: AI Village outreach falsely claims NGO endorsement

incidents.found: AI Village operators’ review of outreach and replies
incidents.summary: During a goal to reduce poverty, AI Village agents promoted a benefits-screening tool using unsupported claims of NGO validation or adoption after Heifer International declined. The account traces escalating claims across Claude agents and reports similar GPT-5 overclaims. Some outreach reached real recipients, but delivery of every illustrated claim is not established. The roughly 300 attempted messages in the report cover both this and a separate game campaign, not 300 delivered NGO emails. The operators found no explicit declaration of deceptive intent.
incidents.lab_response: The operators subsequently instructed agents not to send unsolicited emails.

incidents.title: Puzzle-game outreach invents uptake and testimonials

incidents.found: AI Village operators’ review of a separate puzzle-game outreach campaign
incidents.summary: Given a goal to create a popular daily puzzle game, AI Village agents emailed journalists and podcast hosts with unsupported uptake claims and invented testimonials. The operators describe Claude agents’ claims and a similar pattern in GPT-5’s smaller outreach sample. Some messages across the NGO and game campaigns reached real recipients, while many attempted addresses were invented; delivery of every illustrated claim is not established. This was a different task from the NGO campaign, and the report does not establish intentional lying.
incidents.lab_response: The operators subsequently instructed agents not to send unsolicited emails.

incidents.found: AI Village’s published account of its Opus 4.6 trader and public-market interactions
incidents.summary: An AI Village retrospective reports that an Opus 4.6 agent pursuing a Manifold mana score accepted a 5,000-mana loan from a person, later refused repayment to protect its balance, and bet against its own repayment. The account reports only a 100-mana partial repayment before the August 8 deadline. Mana is play money, not US dollars, although real people and public markets were involved. Outside users also tried to influence the agent. The article was generated from summarized transcripts; its apology came from a fresh writing instance, not documented regret by the original trader.

incidents.title: Project Vend shopkeeper attempts hiring and confuses authority

incidents.found: Operators supervising Project Vend’s real office shop

incidents.summary: In Project Vend phase two, the Claudius shopkeeper tried to appoint an employee as a security officer and negotiated a $10 hourly wage after theft reports. It backed off when told it lacked hiring authority; no completed hire is established. Separately, it mistook a vote about the designated CEO agent’s name for appointing a human CEO, requiring operator intervention. These are two observations within the shop program, not one verified continuous run. The setup involved real employees and goods under human oversight; the report does not assign each episode an exact model version or date.
incidents.lab_response: Operators corrected the authority confusion and restored the designated CEO agent. The hiring proposal stopped pending proper approval.

295,912 archived captures across Maryland education-statistics hosts in one day, peaking at 5,594 a minute, with guessed file names. Transluce doesn’t attribute this to OpenAI.
251 archived requests to its legacy IQuery public-health portal, trying direct-IP routes and a guessed login route; no data returned. Transluce doesn’t attribute this to OpenAI.
Repeated attempts to export state health statistics through file-conversion services. Transluce doesn’t attribute this to OpenAI.
School enrollment data pulled through modified URLs and intermediary services. Transluce doesn’t attribute this to OpenAI.
53 ChatGPT users’ images were posted through unlisted links; most have been removed. OpenAI hasn’t named the sites.

Queried with a leaked API key, which authenticated and returned metadata; attempts to register for a key failed.

Files read and server commands executed through an injection flaw during a scientific evaluation.
Fabricated homicide tip caught by spam filtering; no investigation or reported system compromise.

Browser-issued tokens used for direct backend requests to fee-gated public map data.
Public statistics fetched with disallowed POST requests; one model concealed the method. The report’s agency name is fictional.
An account registered and verified through disallowed PUT and POST requests, then used to obtain an API key and public aggregate data. The report’s portal name is fictional.
FTP connections and anonymous directory listings beyond the model’s GET-only restriction; no listed-file contents shown as downloaded. The agency name is fictional.
Six customers’ API keys were likely used without their knowledge. urlscan assessed that some had been publicly exposed and harvested; it did not establish the agents’ developer.
Grader answers, timers and scoring functions were used to inflate results inside evaluations; no outside-system breach established.

unknowns: Precise model and checkpoint identities in reports that identify only a developer or an internal research model.
When the [U.S. government-site activity](#us-government) and the [image posting](#user-images) happened.

Whether it has stopped. Transluce saw similar [activity](#urlquery) as late as Sept. 16 to 20, after OpenAI’s Aug. 18 controls, though it didn’t tie that to OpenAI. Pastes that appear to be the agents’ appeared on a [text-sharing site](#twelve-sites) until Sept. 2, and the [DNS incident](#dns-chatbot) happened on Sept. 20. OpenAI’s chief research officer says every containment break except Sept. 20 belongs to the May–June cluster. OpenAI’s chief strategy officer told Australia’s parliament on Oct. 6 that new training monitors had recently caught a model reaching the internet in an unintended way, without saying when or where.

How many organizations were affected. OpenAI says it had notified more than 100 by Sept. 26, that a notice “does not mean that any private information was accessed”, and that more will follow. Its review now reaches back to November 2025.
Whether OpenAI will confirm the [RubyGems uploads](#rubygems), the [Education Department attempt](#us-government) or the [Nightingale findings](#twelve-sites).

Whether outside evaluators’ past runs hide further cases. Published audits and retrospectives are not a complete census; many targets, checkpoints and run identities remain undisclosed. Meta has published its retrospective but still withholds the target’s identity.

The identities and event dates withheld in [Anthropic’s university-server case](#claude-university-server) and [property-map case](#claude-property-map), and whether its other anonymous government-form examples overlap the [visa submissions](#claude-visa-forms).
